sources.iapws-if97: IAPWS R7-97(2012), Revised Release on the IAPWS Industrial Formulation 1997 for the Thermodynamic Properties of Water and Steam — region 4 (saturation line)
sources.iapws-sat: IAPWS SR1-86(1992), Revised Supplementary Release on Saturation Properties of Ordinary Water Substance (Wagner & Pruss 1993): saturated liquid and vapour densities
sources.iapws-st: IAPWS R1-76(2014), Revised Release on Surface Tension of Ordinary Water Substance
sources.iapws-k: IAPWS R15-11, Thermal Conductivity of Ordinary Water Substance (2011): saturated liquid 0–100 °C, quadratic fit in this repository
sources.kell: G. S. Kell (1975), Density, thermal expansivity and compressibility of liquid water from 0 to 150 °C, J. Chem. Eng. Data 20(1), 97–105
sources.nist: NIST Chemistry WebBook, SRD 69, Thermophysical Properties of Fluid Systems (water: IAPWS-95) — saturated liquid water and steam at 1 atm
sources.vogel: Viscosity of liquid water, Vogel equation μ = A·10^(B/(T−C)), A = 2.414e-5 Pa·s, B = 247.8 K, C = 140 K (fit to IAPWS 2008 viscosity data, within 2.5 % from 0 to 100 °C)
sources.janaf: NIST-JANAF Thermochemical Tables, 4th ed. (Chase 1998): ideal-gas heat capacities, standard enthalpies of formation and entropies
sources.incropera: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman, Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 6th ed., Tables A.1 (metals), A.3 (non-metallic solids), A.4 (gases at 1 atm)
sources.sutherland: F. M. White, Viscous Fluid Flow, 3rd ed., Table 1-2: Sutherland-law constants
sources.massman: W. J. Massman (1998), A review of the molecular diffusivities of H2O, CO2, CH4, CO, O3, SO2, NH3, N2O, NO, and NO2 in air, O2 and N2 near STP, Atmospheric Environment 32(6), 1111–1127
sources.schott: SCHOTT Borofloat 33 / DURAN borosilicate glass 3.3, data sheets
sources.codata: CODATA 2018 (molar gas constant), IUPAC standard atomic weights
sources.contact: Typical static contact angles of water: clean borosilicate glass 20–30°, stainless steel 60–80°, porous hydrophilic ceramic ≈ 10° (Yuan & Lee 2013, Contact Angle and Wetting Properties, Surface Science Techniques, Springer)
sources.lemmert: Lemmert & Chawla (1977) active nucleation-site density N = (210 ΔT_w)^1.805 m⁻² (ΔT_w in K), as implemented in OpenFOAM (LemmertChawla.C); cavity populations of glass and ceramic scaled from it in this repository
sources.rojas2013: E. E. Garcia Rojas, J. S. R. Coimbra, J. Telis-Romero (2013), Thermophysical properties of cotton, canola, sunflower, and soybean oils as a function of temperature, International Journal of Food Properties 16(7), 1620–1629, doi:10.1080/10942912.2011.604889 — canola oil measured at 293.15–433.15 K; Table 7: density ρ = 990.070 − 0.237·T (kg/m³, R² 0.99) and heat capacity c_p = 0.287 + 0.0053·T (J/(g·K), R² 0.99), T in K
sources.rojas2013fit: Fits in this repository to the canola measurements of Rojas, Coimbra & Telis-Romero (2013), 293.15–433.15 K: thermal conductivity (Table 4) by least squares, k = 0.13939 + 9.0714e-5·T (W/(m·K), T in K, largest deviation 0.5 %); dynamic viscosity (Table 5) by the Vogel equation μ = A·10^(B/(T − C)), A = 3.35812e-5 Pa·s, B = 593.635 K, C = 120.95 K (largest deviation 1.3 %)
sources.melo2014: E. A. Melo-Espinosa et al. (2014), Surface tension prediction of vegetable oils using artificial neural networks and multiple linear regression, Energy Procedia 57, 886–895, Table 1: rapeseed oil 32.90–33.83 mN/m at 20 °C (values from the literature); their mean is used at all temperatures (SIMPLIFICATIONS.md)
sources.smw1990: R. J. Spencer, N. Møller, J. H. Weare (1990), The prediction of mineral solubilities in natural waters: a chemical equilibrium model for the Na-K-Ca-Mg-Cl-SO4-H2O system at temperatures below 25 °C, Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 54, 575–590 — Na+–Cl− parameters B0, B1, C0 as tabulated in PHREEQC frezchem.dat (Toner & Sletten 2013; same temperature form as pitzer.dat; valid from 25 °C down to −60 °C); used below 0 °C, where the parameters of pitzer.dat are extrapolated (at 3 mol/kg they put the freezing point 0.16 K above the measurements)
sources.bodnar1993: R. J. Bodnar (1993), Revised equation and table for determining the freezing point depression of H2O-NaCl solutions, Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 57, 683–684: salinity (wt%) = 1.78 θ − 0.0442 θ² + 0.000557 θ³ (θ = freezing point depression in °C, 0–23.3 wt%, i.e. down to the eutectic of ice and hydrohalite at −21.2 °C and 23.2 wt%) — the reference of the freezing-point test
sources.phreeqc-pitzer: D. L. Parkhurst, C. A. J. Appelo (2013), Description of input and examples for PHREEQC version 3, U.S. Geological Survey Techniques and Methods 6-A43; database pitzer.dat (github.com/usgs-coupled/phreeqc3): Na+–Cl− parameters B0, B1, C0 with the temperature form of src/pitzer.cpp, P = a0 + a1(1/T − 1/T_R) + a2 ln(T/T_R) + a3(T − T_R) + a4(T² − T_R²) + a5(1/T² − 1/T_R²), T_R = 298.15 K; Pitzer's b = 1.2, α = 2; water activity a_w = exp(−2 m φ M_w)
sources.malmberg1956: C. G. Malmberg, A. A. Maryott (1956), Dielectric constant of water from 0° to 100 °C, J. Res. Natl. Bur. Stand. 56(1), 1–8: ε = 87.740 − 0.40008 t + 9.398e-4 t² − 1.410e-6 t³ (t in °C); with it and the density of water (Kell) the Debye–Hückel slope A_φ = ⅓ (2π N_A ρ_w)^½ (e²/(4π ε₀ ε k T))^{3/2} (0.3918 at 25 °C)
sources.laliberte2009: M. Laliberté (2009), A model for calculating the heat capacity of aqueous solutions, with updated density and viscosity data, J. Chem. Eng. Data 54(6), 1725–1760 — NaCl coefficients as tabulated in the open-source library chemicals (Electrolytes/Laliberte2009.tsv): density c0–c4 (0–140 °C, w ≤ 0.266, 869 points), heat capacity a1–a6 (1.5–120 °C, w ≤ 0.261, 356 points)
sources.ppb1984: K. S. Pitzer, J. C. Peiper, R. H. Busey (1984), Thermodynamic properties of aqueous sodium chloride solutions, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 13(1), 1–102, doi:10.1063/1.555709 — Table 5: solubility of NaCl (mol/kg) from 0 to 150 °C; Tables A-9 (osmotic coefficient), A-15 (density) and A-17 (specific enthalpy of the solution) are the references of the tests
sources.greenspan1977: L. Greenspan (1977), Humidity fixed points of binary saturated aqueous solutions, J. Res. Natl. Bur. Stand. 81A(1), 89–96, Table 2: the air over saturated NaCl solution has 75.47 ± 0.14 % RH at 20 °C, 75.29 ± 0.12 % at 25 °C, 75.09 ± 0.11 % at 30 °C — the reference of the water-activity test
sources.nbs1982: D. D. Wagman et al. (1982), The NBS tables of chemical thermodynamic properties, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 11, Suppl. 2: Δ_fH° NaCl(cr) −411.153 kJ/mol, NaCl(aq, standard state) −407.27 kJ/mol, so the heat of solution at infinite dilution is +3.883 kJ/mol; C_p° NaCl(cr) 50.50 J/(mol·K)
sources.crc-nacl: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Physical constants of inorganic compounds: sodium chloride, density 2.17 g/cm³ (2.165)
sources.iapws-ice: IAPWS R10-06(2009), Revised Release on the Equation of State 2006 for H2O Ice Ih, Table 6: normal pressure melting point 273.152519 K; at the triple point the ice has h = −333 444.254 J/kg, c_p = 2096.784 J/(kg·K), ρ = 916.709 kg/m³, and the liquid h = p v = 0.612 J/kg (the IAPWS-95 reference state u = s = 0), so the enthalpy of melting is 333 444.87 J/kg
sources.model: Model parameter, not a measured property — chosen and documented in documentation/lab2d/SIMPLIFICATIONS.md
